native_result.query: What kind of demographic disparities exist in median wealth in 1985 among individuals who were ever incarcerated?
native_result.HypoA: Gender disparities exist in median wealth in 1985 among individuals who were ever incarcerated, with males having higher median wealth than females.
native_result.HypoB: Among the 289 NLSY79 respondents ever incarcerated (jailed 1985-1994), 1985 wealth was essentially nil - median $720 (95% bootstrap CI $0-$1,200) with 45.0% holding zero or negative assets - and the disparities within this group run mainly along race, with a second, bottom-of-the-distribution divide along sex. Median 1985 wealth was $2,200 for ever-incarcerated white respondents, $320 for black respondents, and exactly $0 for hispanic respondents (asset poverty 31.9%, 47.8% and 52.5% respectively); the white-black gap is +$1,880 (permutation p=0.010 but bootstrap CI -127 to +$4,950, so suggestive rather than established) and the black-hispanic difference is negligible ($320, p=0.79). Among men, the only adequately powered race contrast, white men ($2,000, 29.8% at or below zero) held roughly 2.5 times the median wealth of black men ($800, 44.1%) and hispanic men ($700, 46.2%), though neither difference is statistically secure at n=252. The ever-incarcerated female median is literally $0 (n=37; CI degenerate because 64.9% have exactly zero wealth) versus $1,000 for men, and the female-male asset-poverty gap (70.3% vs 41.3%) is the more stable signal than the median gap itself. Race-specific results for women (n=16, 9, 12) are reported but not interpretable, and no race x sex interaction can be supported. Because q10 and q25 are $0 in every race group, the racial gap is invisible at the bottom and appears only as a level shift in the share with nothing, widening in dollars above the median (median -$1,880, q75 -$4,400, p90 -$14,104 for black vs white) while positive-wealth medians nearly converge ($4,400 vs $6,000). Race accounts for somewhat more spread than sex (median range $2,200 vs $1,000; both cuts explain only ~2% of rank variation, Kruskal-Wallis p=0.07 and p=0.02). These are descriptive, within-sample disparities measured at the start of the 1985-1994 incarceration window, so they characterise the wealth profile of people who are incarcerated during the window rather than an effect of incarceration; the flag cannot be cross-validated (no place-of-residence or detention-facility field exists in this file), jail cannot be distinguished from prison or short from long spells, and with no sampling weights and a household survey frame the results do not generalise beyond this NLSY79 sample.
native_result.WorkflowB: Read data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows; 6 columns); relabelled 'hipanic'->'hispanic'; retained all zeros/negatives and the 1,899 duplicate rows; defined the primary population as ever_jailed==1 (n=289) and the never-incarcerated (n=11,724) as reference only. For the primary population computed, overall and by race, sex and race x sex: n, q25, median, q75, p90, IQR, mean, min/max, share with wealth <=0 / ==0 / <0 / >0, and percentile-bootstrap 95% CIs for medians (B=2,000) and for asset-poverty shares (B=4,000; seed 20261022). Added medians restricted to strictly positive wealth, dollar differences and ratios vs the never-incarcerated group in the same demographic cell (ratios only where both medians >0), a q10-q25-median-q75-p90 ladder by race to locate the gap in the distribution, Kruskal-Wallis and rank eta-squared to compare the race and sex cuts, B=20,000 permutation tests for median differences, Mann-Whitney male-only race contrasts, threshold tail shares ($0/$1k/$10k/$50k/$100k), and a clearly-labelled nominal-dollar 1990/1996 trend as robustness only. Applied the agreed thresholds (n>=30 headline; 20-29 indicative, unstable; n<30 shown with n and CIs but excluded from race-specific female conclusions).
